newsitem.title: UK: British Rail regulator calls for new powers.
newsitem.headline: British Rail regulator calls for new powers.

text.p: Britain's Rail Regulator has called on the government to widen significantly his powers, allowing him to regulate the 25 rail franchises and rolling stock companies as well as Railtrack Plc.

John Swift, the Rail Regulator, told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday he believed his office could live alongside the Labour government's planned Strategic Rail Authority (SRA) -- with the Authority setting policy and his watchdog policing the industry.
His call comes as the government decides how to shake-up rail regulation.
Swift said the existing rail franchise regulator OPRAF could be merged into a policy-making SRA, but added this remained "a political decision."
If the new Labour government backs Swift's idea, the rail regulator could have sweeping policing powers over the entire industry.
At present the rail passenger franchises are governed by OPRAF which awards licenses. The rolling stock companies (ROSCOs) are unregulated.
One option under the government's rail review is to bring the multi-billion-pound rolling stock firms under regulatory control for the first time.

"If our powers were extended it could apply to areas like the ROSCOs. At the moment they are not operating in fully competitive markets -- because of their (pre-written) contracts they each enjoy little pockets of monopoly," said Swift.
Swift said a more powerful watchdog could tackle three areas.

"First, it can stand between Railtrack and the independent TOCs (train operating companies or franchises). Second, it can ensure the TOCs have every opportunity to innovate and co-operate to provide network wide benefits.
"Third it can promote the interests of freight and monitor the development of services, influencing its structure."
Swift denied there would be an overlap between the government's SRA and an independent regulator.
"It does not necessarily follow that the SRA should be the enforcer as well as policy maker."

Turning to industry standards, Swift said the privatisation process, carried out under the previous Conservative government, had been desperate to encourage players into rail. "It was keen to bring people in and so it set minimum standards, leaving the market to develop as it thought fit."
He said at present passengers remained sceptical when "a regulator says to the TOCs 'stick to the letter of the law and you'll be alright'."
In his own patch, Swift recently hardened his stance against Railtrack, the infrastructure group which owns track, stations and signalling, on its spending plans.

Commenting on the recent climbdown by Railtrack to agree to a license amendment, he said, "It's very important...It is similar to what Don Cruickshank (the telecoms regulator) wanted from BT (British Telecommunications Plc).
"But he was asking for it on anti-competition grounds. I want it on the grounds of monitoring Railtrack's (investment) performance."

"Before this, if Railtrack was taken over tomorrow, the new owner could look at its plans for one billion pounds ($1.7 billion) of investment a year and say to Railtrack 'Go and tell the regulator to push off.' What we've got now is a sanction to ensure that the money is spent. It's in the public interest."
